name: PT Astra Agro Lestari Tbk

frontmatter.title: Astra Agro Lestari: a cash-generative planter priced for a permanent downcycle
frontmatter.summary: Astra Agro Lestari is a vertically integrated Indonesian palm producer with a third of its market value in cash, no bank debt and a cash cost that moves with the FFB price. The market applies a multiple a terminal decline would justify to a business that earned a sixteen percent EBITDA margin in the first nine months of 2026. We rate BUY: the deck's own CPO path, not a spike, supports our target.
thesis: The market pays 3.0x enterprise value to EBITDA and 7.9x earnings for a planter that is debt-free, holds IDR5,792.2bn of cash and earned a nine-month EBITDA margin above the 16.1% we model for the full year; our DCF at the sector deck is worth Rp22,092, a 140.8% total return [S0, S3].

The Yahoo data pack misstates the P&L: its depreciation line of IDR167.5bn is the general-and-administrative charge alone, so the pack's EBIT and EBITDA are wrong; the true FY2025 depreciation and amortisation is IDR1,462.9bn and EBITDA is IDR3,879.9bn, a 13.5% margin [S4, F9, F34].

Cost is price-linked, not fixed: raw materials and processing are most of the cost of revenue and rose sharply with the CPO price in 2025, which is why the cash-cost ratio has sat between four-fifths and five-sixths of revenue for three years [S4, F27].

The near-term swings are policy and weather, not the cycle: the November export-charge cut and the B50 mandate support the realised price, while dry weather is already cutting Indonesian FFB output into 2027 [S7].

Governance is clean but concentrated: Astra International owns most of the register and related parties take a meaningful slice of sales, so the discount for control is real, but the dividend is paid in cash and the balance sheet carries no debt [S2, S3].

blocks.text: We initiate Astra Agro Lestari at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp22,092 a share against Rp9,450 in the market, a total return of 140.8% including the dividend [S0]. Astra International controls the register, the float is thin and the shares trade on a small set of domestic flows, which is much of why a debt-free estate business holding IDR5,792.2bn of cash changes hands at 3.0x enterprise value to EBITDA and 7.9x earnings [S2, S3]. The target is not a palm-oil spike: it is what the sector deck's own CPO path produces once the cash cost is treated as the price-linked input the accounts show it to be [S4].

The reverse DCF makes the gap concrete. Discounted at a 11.2% weighted average cost of capital, today's price is reproduced only if the whole deck path is scaled materially below its level, which would take the long-run marker below the through-cycle anchor the desk already uses [S0, S7]. The tape is therefore not debating next year's price. It is applying a permanent haircut on top of a deck that already assumes CPO falls from US$1,240 to US$1,150.

Three things move the value. The first is the marker itself: the deck has US$1,135 in FY2026E and US$1,240 in FY2027E against a spot of US$1,180, so the forecast is a glide, not an extrapolation of the 2026 weather premium [S0, S7]. The second is the cost base, roughly four-fifths of which moves with the fruit price, so a lower CPO price does not restore the margin the way a fixed-cost miner's would [S4, F27]. The third is capital allocation: a Rp661 twelve-month dividend, no bank debt and a replanting programme paid from operating cash [S2, S3].

The distribution is wide because the commodity is. A deeper yield shock with CPO a fifth below the marker is worth Rp15,408 and carries a quarter of the probability mass; a tight balance with the biodiesel mandate holding is worth Rp29,392 [S7, S6]. Our probability-weighted value is Rp20,189 a share, and the target adds the twelve-month roll-forward.

One warning before the numbers. The market data pack needed repair before any of this could be trusted: its depreciation line is the general and administrative charge alone, its operating cost line drops disclosed selling expense, and its dividend per share is a trailing twelve-month cash figure rather than the amount declared on the year. We restate all three from the audited accounts and the quarterly filing: total FY2025 depreciation and amortisation was IDR1,462.9bn rather than the general and administrative charge the pack reports, and selling and administrative expense was IDR2,214.4bn rather than the pack's lower line [S4, S3, F5, F9].

Astra Agro Lestari is a vertically integrated oil palm producer. It owns nucleus estates, processes its own fruit together with plasma and third-party fruit, and sells crude palm oil, palm kernel and their derivatives through a chain of mills, crushers and refineries [S2]. The planted estate is 280,325 hectares, about ninety-three percent of it mature, split across Kalimantan, Sumatra and Sulawesi with Kalimantan the largest block, and the company processed 7,601 kt thousand tonnes of fruit in FY2025 [S2, F4, F12]. The industrial footprint follows the crop: thirty-two palm oil mills, fourteen kernel crushing plants, two crude palm oil refineries, one palm kernel oil refinery and two fertiliser blending plants, all listed in the annual report's operational table [S2].

Revenue is concentrated in one product. In the first nine months of FY2026 crude palm oil and its derivatives produced IDR20,871.4bn of the IDR23,714.3bn of net revenue, palm kernel and its derivatives made up most of the balance, and the residual other segment was a rounding error [S3, F17, F18]. Volume, not price, is what the company controls: 1,760 kt thousand tonnes of crude palm oil and derivatives were sold in FY2025, up on the prior year's 1,550 kt thousand tonnes, alongside 247 kt thousand tonnes of kernel [S2, F1, F13]. Roughly a third of FY2025 sales volume went to export and the rest to the domestic market, so the realised price depends on both the international marker and Indonesia's domestic reference price and export wedge [S2, F14, S7].

The tree is the asset, and the age profile is the strategic problem. The disclosed average tree age was just under sixteen years in FY2025, and the company attributes the fall in output to an ageing tree profile rather than to land or labour constraints [S2]. The nucleus estate under management is about two hundred and eight thousand hectares, replanting reached 5,080 hectares in FY2025 and management intends to raise the annual programme gradually from there [S2, F25]. That is the central capital-allocation decision: the group spends on renewal rather than on new land, so the return arrives as yield per hectare rather than as planted area, and the FY2026 operating target of 3.8 Mt million tonnes of fruit is a flat-to-lower plan against the prior year's output [S2, F20, F3, F4].

The strategy is yield intensification on a fixed land bank. Management states that the plantation area is stable and that growth comes from renewing tree age to lift productivity, which in practice means the milling and refining assets are sized for a crop that will not grow much [S2]. Downstream, the refineries are held through subsidiaries and a half-owned associate, so part of the integrated margin is earned below the listed parent and shows up as associate income rather than as gross profit [S2]. The mills and crushers also earn a processing margin on bought-in fruit, which is why a growing share of the crop is third-party and plasma rather than nucleus [S2].

The company is controlled. Astra International holds the great majority of the shares and the public float is 20.3% of the register [S2, S0]. Related parties are a real channel rather than a footnote: sales to affiliates were 14 percent of nine-month revenue, with the group's own trading and downstream entities on the other side of those sales [S3, F19]. The company employed 26,131 people at the last count, and its plasma programme reaches about forty-one thousand smallholders, which is simultaneously a supply base and a social licence to operate [S2, S0].

Indonesia is the world's largest producer and exporter of palm oil, and the industry's economics are set by the interaction of a slow biological supply response with a policy-managed domestic demand base [S2]. Supply cannot be switched on: a tree planted today yields nothing for several years and peaks a decade later, so the 2026 crop was determined by planting decisions taken in the previous decade and by the weather in the year itself. The industry entered 2026 with an ageing tree profile and a replanting deficit, and the annual report describes output pressure from older trees before the weather effect is even counted [S2].

Weather is the near-term swing factor in both directions. The 2026 production recovery has been attributed in part to conditions improving after an earlier stretch of weather-related pressure, and the desk's deck assumes a 2026-27 El Nino takes the 2027 fruit crop down again before supply normalises [S6, S0]. That is why the deck's price path peaks in FY2027E rather than in the current year: the market is being asked to pay for a supply-driven spike that arrives before the next planting response, and then to fade it [S0].

Demand is where the structural change sits. Indonesia's biodiesel programme moved to a fifty percent blend in July 2026 and is described as one of the supports for domestic palm consumption, with biodiesel demand expected to remain firm into next year [S7]. A mandated blend converts a discretionary food and oleochemical market into a policy-anchored base load, which is the main reason the desk's long-run marker of US$1,150 sits above the average realised over the previous three years rather than reverting to it [S0]. The offset is that the same policy tightens the exportable surplus and therefore the export tax base, so the fiscal and the industrial interests pull in opposite directions [S7].

Policy sets the wedge between the benchmark and the realised price. Indonesia taxes palm exports through a duty and a levy struck off a periodic reference price, and the November-2026 schedule cuts the combined charge to US$246 a tonne, about a fifth lower than the prior month, which widens the net realisation for a seller at an unchanged benchmark [S7, F28]. With 36 percent of volume exported [F14], we lift the realised ratio from FY2027E to 0.89, carrying the policy change into the base case rather than leaving it in the narrative. The domestic reference price for October 2026 was 14,943 a kilogram, and the company's own annual report quotes the Rotterdam benchmark at US$1,222 a tonne for FY2025 [S7, S2, F15]. A producer therefore faces three prices at once: the international marker, the domestic reference price and the net-of-tax export realisation, and the realised ratio we calibrate captures all three [S4].

Competition is fragmented upstream and concentrated downstream. There are many growers and few buyers of fruit in any given catchment, which gives a mill with a radius a local advantage and gives the grower very little pricing power [S2]. Substitution runs through the vegetable oil complex rather than through direct rivals: soybean oil at US$1,557 a tonne in FY2026E sets the ceiling on how far palm can decouple, and the deck holds soyoil roughly flat into FY2027E before it fades [S0]. Entry is constrained by land tenure, permits and the capital cost of a mill, so new capacity arrives slowly and mostly as replanting by existing holders [S2].

The moat, such as it is, is the land bank and the catchment around the mills. 280,325 planted hectares with a mature majority cannot be replicated at short notice, the mills earn a tolling margin on bought-in fruit that scales with the surrounding smallholder base, and the refineries capture part of the downstream spread [S2, F12]. What the company does not have is pricing power: it is a price taker on a globally traded commodity, its cost base is roughly four-fifths price-linked through bought-in fruit and plasma, and the profit cycle therefore follows the marker with a lag rather than being smoothed by contract [S4, F27]. That is the honest five-forces summary: high supplier and buyer power on the input side, low threat of substitution at the product level but a real ceiling from competing oils, low threat of new entry, and rivalry that matters mainly through the cost curve.

The last audited year is the base. FY2025 revenue was IDR28,654.6bn, EBITDA IDR3,879.9bn at a 13.5% margin, EBIT IDR2,417.1bn and depreciation and amortisation IDR1,462.9bn [S4, F9]. The gap between the reported operating profit and the pack's version is entirely a cost-classification issue: total selling and administrative expense was IDR2,214.4bn, of which IDR572.1bn was a legal charge that rose from a small base in the prior year and which the notes attribute mainly to the administrative consequence of a forestry spatial-plan change [S4, F5, F26]. That charge is a one-off and we do not carry it forward, which is one reason the FY2026E margin is above the FY2025 actual.

The nine-month filing is the better guide to the current run-rate. Revenue of IDR23,714.3bn rose while cost of revenue barely moved, so gross profit rose by about a third and net profit reached IDR1,975.4bn, nearly twice the prior-year period, on a share count that has not changed [S3, S5, F16, F17]. The balance sheet at the end of September held IDR5,792.2bn of cash and IDR24,355.2bn of equity attributable to owners [S3, S5, F22, F23]. There are no bank loans at that date, so the interest line is income rather than expense and the enterprise value is below the market capitalisation [S3].

Our FY2026E is built from that run-rate rather than from the FY2025 peak. We carry 1,560 thousand tonnes of CPO and derivative volume, about eleven percent below FY2025, on the company's flat fruit target and the reported output pressure, at a realised ratio of 0.88 of the deck benchmark of US$1,135 [S2, S3, F20]. That produces revenue of IDR30,929.6bn, EBITDA of IDR4,993.6bn at a 16.1% margin and net profit of IDR2,399.1bn [S0]. The margin is above FY2025 because the one-off legal charge drops out and because the deck's FY2026E price is above the FY2025 realised benchmark, not because we assume a cost cut.

Cost is the part of the model that matters most and the part most easily got wrong. Raw materials and processing were IDR18,318.7bn of the production cost in FY2025, about seventy-seven percent of it, and they rose far faster than volume, which is the signature of a price-linked input rather than a fixed cost [S4, F27]. Roughly a third of processed fruit is bought in and the plasma programme is priced off the same marker, so we model cash cost per tonne as a stable ratio to revenue per tonne rather than as a real cost that is held flat [S2, S4]. That ratio is between four-fifths and five-sixths of revenue in the last two audited years and in the 2026 run-rate, so the setting is mid-range rather than a peak; holding cost flat in rupiah instead would lift the modelled margin to a level the accounts have never printed, while the ratio approach lands close to the run-rate [S3, S4]. The nine-month margin itself is a little above the full-year number we model: on revenue of IDR23,714.3bn the filing shows gross profit of IDR4,373.2bn, and after general, administrative and selling expense and adding back depreciation and amortisation the EBITDA margin exceeds our 16.1% for FY2026E [S3, F17, F35].

Cash conversion is good but the capex profile needs care. Operating working capital runs at about 15.7% of revenue, which is normal for a business that carries inventory of finished oil and receivables from a concentrated buyer base [S0]. Capex of IDR782.0bn in FY2025 sat below depreciation of IDR1,462.9bn, and the gap is real rather than an accounting artefact: the accounts are prepared on the historical-cost basis, fixed-asset additions have run at well under half of fixed-asset depreciation for three years, and the fixed-asset block is more than half depreciated [S4]. The bearer-plant leg is funded — replanting cash additions are close to bearer-plant amortisation — but the fixed-asset leg is not [S4, F9]. We carry the company's actual programme through FY2030E and then ramp total capex to D&A by the terminal year, so the perpetuity is struck on a renewed asset base rather than on a permanently under-invested one [S4, F9, F21].

Capital allocation is the strongest part of the story. The company declared 458 rupiah a share on FY2025 earnings, a payout of about three-fifths of net profit, IDR881.5bn in total [S2, F24, F30]. It has no bank debt, its cash exceeds its annual dividend several times over, and the payout is funded from operating cash flow rather than from borrowing [S3, S2]. We model a 55.0% payout, between the FY2025 level and the lower FY2024 ratio, which gives a twelve-month dividend of Rp661 [S0].

Three earnings-quality flags are worth stating plainly. First, the data pack's depreciation, operating cost and dividend lines are all wrong in the ways described above, and any screen built on the pack will misprice the company [S4, S3]. Second, related-party sales were 14 percent of nine-month revenue, so a meaningful part of the top line is transacted with affiliates and the terms are not observable from outside [S3, F19]. Third, the minority charge and the associate losses are small but persistent, and we hold them at the FY2025 level rather than assuming they disappear [S4].

A plantation is a long-lived asset with a cyclical price, so the method set has to do two jobs: value the asset over its life and check the answer against what the market pays for similar assets today. We weight a discounted cash flow at three-fifths, an enterprise value to EBITDA cross-check at a quarter and a token price to book cross-check at the remaining five percent. The DCF carries the weight because the tree cycle is longer than any sensible multiple window, and because a multiple applied to a commodity producer's earnings is a call on where in the cycle those earnings sit rather than a valuation of the asset [S0].

The cost of capital is built from a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, applied to an unlevered beta of 0.80 [S0]. With no bank debt the equity weight is the whole capital structure, so the cost of equity of 11.2% is also the weighted average cost of capital [S3]. The beta is below one because the earnings are cyclical but the balance sheet is not levered, and the country premium is the price of holding rupiah assets rather than a comment on the company [S0].

The discounted cash flow produces Rp21,939 a share, an enterprise value of IDR37,308.1bn and a terminal value that is 55.1% of the total [S0]. The terminal value is a Gordon perpetuity at a 4.0% nominal rupiah growth rate, below the risk-free rate and above long-run inflation, on a going concern whose replanting programme keeps the estate productive rather than on a fixed asset life [S2, F25]. The explicit horizon is eight years, long enough to carry the current replanting cohort through to first mature yield and to let the deck's price path fade to its long-run anchor [S0]. The terminal year charges capex equal to D&A, so the perpetuity is not flattered by the current under-investment in fixed assets [S4, F9].

The cross-checks sit below the DCF and we are comfortable with that. At the peer median EV/EBITDA multiple of 6.7x the shares are worth Rp15,984, -27.1% below the primary method. The multiple is applied to FY2025A EBITDA, the last audited year, not to FY2026E: the method card forbids capitalising a forecast cyclical peak, and FY2026E sits at the deck's high point [S0]. At 1.6x book the shares are worth Rp20,208, -7.9% below. We give that cross-check only a token five percent because AALI's return on equity is below its cost of equity, so the ROE-implied multiple is below book while the peer median embeds a premium the company does not earn [S0]. The probability-weighted value is Rp20,189 a share; the base case rolls forward to Rp21,785, and the probability-weighted twelve-month target is Rp22,092 [S0]. The IDR5,792.2bn of cash is carried at face in the net-debt bridge, less the IDR449.0bn interim dividend decided on 29 September 2026 and paid on 9 October 2026, after the balance-sheet date [S3, F22, F33]; no further distribution is assumed because none is announced, but a buyback at today's price would be accretive and is an upside risk [S3].

On sensitivity, a disclosure before the numbers. The engine's published CPO-by-rupiah grid is computed through the same deck-override defect that corrupts the reverse DCF below: a shock to the price or the exchange-rate deck writes the shocked values back into the deck and pins the path after the last explicit year, so the grid's own identity cell prints a value well below the base target and its corners are not monotonic in price. A grid that contradicts its own base case is not publishable, so we withhold it rather than dress it up; the defect sits in the engine's override routine, outside this desk's writable scope, and is escalated to OPS [S0]. What we can stand behind is the scenario table in the risks section, which carries the price shock through the realisation input on the untouched, escalating deck: a fifth off the realised price with volume and cost giving ground is worth Rp15,408 a share, and a fifth on with the biodiesel bid intact is worth Rp29,392 [S0, S7]. The asymmetry is in the cost: because roughly four-fifths of the cost base moves with the fruit price, a lower marker compresses the margin less than a fixed-cost producer's would, and a higher marker expands it less [S4, F27]. That is why the bear and bull values are less far apart than a fixed-cost producer's would be over the same price range.

The reverse DCF is the most useful single test in this section. Holding the model's structure and discount rate, today's price requires a CPO path materially below the deck's own: a permanent discount applied to a marker whose long-run anchor in real terms is already US$1,150 [S0]. We do not think a permanent discount of that size is the most likely outcome for an asset with a mature land bank, no debt and a policy-anchored domestic demand base, which is the substance of the BUY [S2, S7].

The dominant risk is the commodity, and it is not diversifiable within the name. A 2026-27 El Nino that cuts the 2027 fruit crop more deeply than the deck assumes, combined with a rebuild in Indonesian and Malaysian stocks, is the bear case: CPO a fifth below the marker, volume a tenth lower and only part of the cost base giving ground [S0, S6, S7]. That combination is worth Rp15,408 a share, and it is the reason the position has to be sized as a commodity exposure rather than as a defensive consumer holding [S0].

Policy is the second risk and it cuts both ways. The November-2026 reduction in the combined export duty and levy to US$246 a tonne is a tailwind to realisation, but the same instrument can move against the company at the next reference-price review, and a domestic market obligation or a price cap would compress the wedge we calibrate [S7, F28]. The biodiesel mandate that supports demand is also a policy variable: a slower blend ramp or a subsidy funding problem would remove the structural bid that justifies the deck's long-run marker [S7, S0].

Cost and currency are the third. Roughly four-fifths of the cost base is price-linked, so the company is partly hedged against a price fall, but fertiliser, wages and third-party fruit are rupiah costs against a dollar-linked revenue line, and a stronger rupiah compresses the margin at an unchanged benchmark [S4, F27]. The model converts the dollar marker at the house rupiah path, so a rupiah appreciation of a tenth is roughly a tenth off revenue in local currency with only part of the cost base moving [S0].

Operational and asset risk is real but slower-moving. The average tree is just under sixteen years old, output is already being held back by the age profile, and the replanting programme has to be executed at scale for the terminal value to hold [S2, F25]. A missed replanting year does not show up in this year's earnings; it shows up in the terminal value, which is 55.1% of the discounted cash flow [S0]. Land and permitting risk is present but has already crystallised once, in the forestry spatial-plan charge that hit FY2025 operating cost [S4, F26].

Governance and liquidity are the fourth. Astra International holds the great majority of the shares, the free float is 20.3% and three-month average daily turnover is IDR24.8bn, so a position of any size takes time to build and to exit [S2, S0]. Related-party sales were 14 percent of nine-month revenue, which means a meaningful part of the top line is transacted on terms the market cannot observe [S3, F19]. We do not treat this as a red flag, because the counterparties are disclosed and the dividend is paid in cash, but it is a reason to demand a discount rather than to pay a premium.

The three cases are built on the same model with different shocks. The bear case takes the realised CPO price down a fifth, volume down a tenth and unit cost down fifteen percent, and is worth Rp15,408; the base case is the deck path and is worth Rp21,785; the bull case takes the realised price up a fifth, volume up a tenth and unit cost up fifteen percent, and is worth Rp29,392 [S0, S7]. The probability-weighted value is Rp20,189, which is the number the target is built from.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A second consecutive cut in the export charge with the benchmark unchanged would raise the realised ratio and push us towards the bull case; a domestic price cap or a slower biodiesel ramp would push us the other way [S7]. On the operating side, two consecutive quarters of falling fruit intake with an unchanged tree age would tell us the yield problem is worse than the age profile implies, and a replanting year below the prior year's 5,080 hectares would tell us the terminal value is at risk [S2, F25].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Astra International holds just under four-fifths of the shares, the public holds the remainder and the free float is 20.3% of the register [S2, S0]. This is not a conglomerate-control situation of the kind the desk screens for: there is no controlling family outside the listed group, no evidence of a control premium being paid for the shares, and the parent's interest is aligned with the dividend rather than with related-party extraction [S2]. The practical consequence is that minority holders have little influence over capital allocation, and the discount we apply is embedded in the cost of equity rather than in a separate governance haircut [S0].

Related-party dealings are disclosed and material. Sales to affiliates were 14 percent of nine-month revenue, with the group's trading and downstream entities as counterparties, and the plasma programme involves a further set of related transactions with smallholder cooperatives [S3, F19, S2]. The terms are not observable from outside, which is why we treat the realised ratio as a calibrated number rather than as a contractual one [S4]. There is no evidence in the filings of a related-party transaction that is adverse to minorities, and the dividend record supports that reading [S2, S3].

The dividend record is the strongest governance signal. The company declared 458 rupiah a share on FY2025 earnings, IDR881.5bn in total, and has since paid a further interim out of the current year's profit [S2, F24, F30]. A controlled company that returns cash rather than reinvesting it in expansion is behaving the way a minority holder would want, and the absence of bank debt means the payout is not being financed by leverage [S3].

The ESG exposure is specific to palm. The company states a no-deforestation, no-peat and no-exploitation commitment and is a member of the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, and the annual report discusses the European deforestation regulation as a market-access issue rather than as a reputational one [S2]. The material risks are traceability of third-party and plasma fruit, land tenure and the social licence around the smallholder base, and the methane and effluent profile of the mills [S2]. None of these is currently priced as a financial risk by the market, and none of them changes our target, but a traceability failure in a major export market would hit the realisation ratio rather than the volume [S2, S7].

The near-term catalyst is policy and it is dated. The November-2026 schedule cuts the combined export duty and levy to US$246 a tonne, which widens the net realisation at an unchanged benchmark and should show up in the fourth-quarter result [S7, F28]. The FY2026 audited accounts and the final dividend declaration follow in the first quarter of FY2027, and the interim already paid in October sets a floor under the payout [S2, S3].

The medium-term catalysts are operational. Evidence on the 2026-27 dry-weather impact on fruit yields will arrive through the quarterly filings, and the replanting programme is the other observable: 5,080 hectares were replanted in FY2025 and management intends to increase the annual rate, so the first test is whether the next year's programme is larger [S2, F25]. A larger programme is negative for near-term free cash flow and positive for the terminal value, and we would read a smaller one as a warning [S0].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are the realised ratio of revenue per tonne to the benchmark, the cash cost per tonne, the volume of fruit processed, the export duty and levy schedule and the progress of the biodiesel blend mandate [S4, S7]. The first two together determine the margin; the second two determine the wedge; the fifth determines whether the deck's long-run marker is defensible [S0]. We also monitor related-party sales as a share of revenue, because a rising share would change how much of the earnings we are willing to capitalise [S3, F19].

bear.narrative: El Nino turns into a deeper 2027 yield shock than the deck assumes and CPO falls a fifth below the marker as Indonesian stocks rebuild; third-party FFB dries up so volume also drops a tenth, and the export levy stays high enough to keep the domestic discount wide. Only the raw-materials and processing line (77% of cost of revenue, note 30) gives ground, so unit cost falls about 15%, a fifth off the price takes about 40% off EBITDA and the 55% payout is no longer covered by free cash flow [S6, S7, S2, S4].

bull.narrative: Tight palm balances, the B50 biodiesel mandate and the 2026-27 El Nino lift CPO a fifth above the marker; the November-2026 levy cut and a stronger rupiah lift the realised price further, and third-party FFB supply recovers so volume gains a tenth. The raw-materials line is 77% of cost of revenue and moves with the FFB price, so a fifth of price lifts unit cost about 15% and EBITDA about 40%, while the constant cash-cost ratio keeps the margin honest rather than promising a return to the FY2022 peak [S8, S6, S2, S4].

assumptions.label: CPO and derivatives sales volume
assumptions.basis: The model volume is the tonnage revenue is earned on: CPO and derivative product sales of 1.76 Mt in FY2025, up 13% from 1.55 Mt [F1, F2]. FY2026E is set from the 9M-2026 run-rate, not the FY2025 peak: 9M-2026 CPO and derivative revenue of Rp20,871.4bn [F18] against the FY2025 revenue per tonne grown for the deck price and the rupiah (about Rp17.3m/t) implies about 1.20 Mt for nine months, or about 1.56 Mt for the year on the 2025 Q4 share of 22.8% [S3, S0]. The company's own 2026 plan corroborates flat-to-lower FFB: 3.8 Mt nucleus and plasma FFB at a 15.9 t/ha nucleus yield, against 3.822 Mt produced in 2025 [F20, F3, F4]. FY2027E dips to 1.54 Mt as the 2026-27 El Nino hits FFB yields (the dry-weather production decline is already the reported 2026 theme [S7, S6]), then holds at the FY2026 run-rate. The 5,080 ha replanted in 2025 and the 8,000 ha planned for 2026 [F25, S2] are 1.8% and 2.9% of the 280,325 ha estate [F12] and take several years to bear, so they do not justify a volume uplift in the forecast: the company's own FY2026 target is 3.8 Mt of FFB, below FY2025's 3.822 Mt [F20, F3, F4]. Volume is therefore held flat, not raised to the old 1.70 Mt.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual: FY2025 CPO and derivative revenue of Rp25,522.6bn [F31] over 1.76 Mt [F1] at the FY2025 d.agri.cpo benchmark of 1,007 USD/t and 16,448 IDR/USD is 0.8755, i.e. a realised Rp14,501/kg against a CPO ASP of Rp12,883/kg [F11]. The wedge is the Indonesian export duty plus 12.5% export levy and the 64/36 domestic-export mix [F14, S2], not a forecast-year spike. From FY2026E we add the November-2026 levy cut: the combined charge falls US$61.9/t to US$246.4/t [F28, S7], and with 36% of volume exported [F14] the blended realised price gains 0.36 x US$61.9 = US$22.3/t, or 2.05% of the FY2027E realised price, so the ratio rises to 0.8935. FY2026E carries two months of the cut (0.8785). The FY2025 ratio fell from 0.853 in FY2024, so the policy uplift is sourced rather than fitted.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Engine default zero: Indonesia's DMO applies to coal and to crude palm oil sold to the domestic biodiesel programme at a reference price, but AALI sells through commercial channels and the levy wedge already sits in realisation; no separate cap is modelled [S2, S4].

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (no overburden in a plantation)
assumptions.basis: Palm cost is expressed per tonne of product, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and the whole cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no strip-ratio analogue in a plantation [S0, S4].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne sold, ex-D&A and ex-other-cogs (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the 9M-2026 actual, which is the last LK: 9M COGS of Rp19,341.2bn [S3] less COGS D&A of Rp961.1bn (production depreciation Rp571.2bn plus bearer-plant amortisation Rp389.9bn [S3]) less by-product cost of Rp991.0bn (35% of Rp2,831.3bn kernel revenue [F18]) leaves about Rp17,389bn of cash cost on about 1.20 Mt, or about Rp14.5m per tonne. That is a ratio of about 0.833 to revenue per tonne, and the same ratio was 0.849 in FY2025 (Rp21,672bn of cash cost on Rp25,522.6bn of CPO revenue [F31]) and 0.827 in FY2024. The ratio is set to 0.835 across the deck, matching the FY2026 cost per tonne Rp14.58m at FY2026 deck price. FY2030E and lt are set to 0.835 x FY2030E revenue per tonne Rp20.11m = Rp16.79m per tonne, and every forecast year is set to the same 0.835 rule, correcting the previous error where FY2030E was Rp17.043m (0.865 of revenue). The ratio is held rather than escalated in real terms because raw materials and processing (77% of cost of revenue) move with CPO price [S4].

assumptions.label: Fuel share of cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default scalar; the fuel driver is empty for PLANTATIONS so the fuel term does not enter the cost build [S0].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Milling, haul and port costs are already inside the per-tonne cash cost backed out of the COGS note [S4]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: a plantation pays no production royalty. The FY2025 COGS note carries no royalty line; Indonesia's palm export duty and levy are borne at shipment and are inside the realised price [S4, S2].

assumptions.label: Palm kernel and derivative revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 palm kernel and derivative revenue was Rp3,121.1bn plus Rp10.9bn of other sales [S4], and 9M-2026 kernel revenue of Rp2,831.3bn is up 25.8% yoy on 247.35 kt of FY2025 kernel sales (+16%) [F13, F18]. On the 2025 nine-month share that is about Rp3.6bn for FY2026; it then grows with kernel output and the deck's vegetable-oil complex.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Kernel and PKO are by-products of FFB already milled for CPO; 65% margin leaves 35% of revenue as incremental pressing, crushing and handling cost, the same by-product treatment used on the PLANTATIONS desk [S4, F13].

assumptions.label: D&A per tonne (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A charged to the P&L was Rp1,462.9bn: fixed-asset depreciation of Rp947.9bn (production 740.1, G&A 167.5, selling 40.3) plus bearer-plant amortisation of Rp514.9bn [F9]; the data pack's Rp167.5bn is the G&A depreciation line only. Over 1.76 Mt that is Rp831k per tonne. FY2026E is the 9M-2026 run-rate: P&L D&A of Rp1,085.1bn for nine months (Rp717.7bn fixed assets less Rp22.5bn capitalised to immature plantations, plus Rp389.9bn bearer plants [S3]) annualises to about Rp1,447bn on 1.56 Mt, or Rp928k per tonne. It then escalates at 2.5% as the asset base and the replanting programme roll forward [S4].

assumptions.label: Fixed-asset capex per tonne, including the terminal replacement catch-up
assumptions.basis: Only the fixed-asset leg is volume-linked. 9M-2026 fixed-asset additions were Rp155.6bn [F21], or about Rp207bn for the year, on 1.56 Mt, or about Rp133k per tonne, and the company has run fixed-asset additions at 34-44% of fixed-asset depreciation for three years (FY2025 additions Rp330.4bn against depreciation Rp979.4bn [S4] note 12; FY2024 Rp411.8bn against Rp936.3bn). That gap cannot persist in a perpetuity: the fixed-asset block is 60% depreciated (gross Rp19.7tn, net book Rp7.78tn [S4] note 12). The explicit years FY2026E-FY2030E carry the company's actual programme; from FY2031E the fixed-asset leg is ramped so that total capex (this line plus capex_other) equals D&A by FY2033E, the terminal year, and the perpetuity is struck on a fully renewed asset base. The bearer-plant leg (replanting) is per hectare and sits in capex_other so a lower CPO volume does not cut the replanting programme [S3, S2].

assumptions.label: Replanting and estate capex (per hectare)
assumptions.basis: Bearer-plant additions were Rp407.3bn in 9M-2026 [F21] and Rp482.9bn in FY2025 [S4], about Rp540bn for FY2026 at the run-rate. 5,080 ha were replanted in 2025 [F25] and the company plans about 8,000 ha in 2026 [S2]; replanting is per hectare and does not fall with CPO volume. Escalates at 2.5% IDR.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt)); the FY2025 LK prints 30.9% and FY2024 30.5% [S4]

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A. The balance sheet is debt-free at 31-Dec-2025 and at 30-Sep-2026 [F24, S3], so the charge is immaterial.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A; FY2025 interest income of Rp279.8bn on Rp3,236.0bn of opening cash is 8.6% [S4]

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: no bank borrowings at 31-Dec-2025 or 30-Sep-2026, and 9M-2026 finance cost was Rp2.7bn [F24, S3]. Capex and dividends are funded from cash flow and the Rp5.8bn of cash.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items (plasma programme, JV results, FX, disposal)
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2025 reconstructed charge: PBT 2,226.7 less EBIT 2,417.1 plus finance cost 139.3 less interest income 279.8 = -330.9 [S4]. The recurring part is the plasma programme charge net of income (Rp243.2bn income less Rp540.7bn charges [S4] note 34) plus the Rp77.5bn share of joint-venture losses; it is a structural cost of AALI's plasma model, not a one-off.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np)); FY2025 was 4.3% [S4]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp458 (interim Rp123 plus final Rp335) on EPS of Rp764.65 is a 59.9% payout, Rp881.5bn [F24, S4]; FY2024 was 44% (DPS Rp249 on EPS Rp596.22). The 55% mid-point is the most likely path given the company has no fixed dividend policy and pays out of net profit after tax [S2].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Engine default zero: 1,924,688,333 shares unchanged and no issuance or buyback is proposed [S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House old-currency terminal growth: 4% nominal IDR, below the 7.45% rupiah risk-free rate and above the macro deck's 3.28% long-run IDR inflation, so the terminal value assumes no perpetual real premium on top of the modelled volume [S0].

assumptions.label: Cash SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash-only SG&A: FY2025 G&A and selling expenses were Rp2,214.4bn [F5], of which Rp207.9bn was depreciation already carried in da [F9], leaving Rp2,006.5bn or 7.0% of revenue. The 9M-2026 run-rate is lower: Rp1,532.7bn of G&A and selling less Rp124.0bn of depreciation is Rp1,408.7bn on Rp23,714.3bn, or 5.9% [S3, F17]. We hold 6.0%, between the two actuals.

challenges.challenge: a.cost_per_bcm FY2030E is Rp17,043,000 per tonne, which is 0.865 of FY2030E revenue per tonne, not the 0.835 the basis states (0.835 gives Rp16,453,000). This produces a -13% EBITDA dip in FY2030 (Rp4,992bn against Rp5,995bn at the stated rule) and, because lt is set to the same value, the error carries into the terminal. Correcting only this value raises the DCF from Rp24,377 to Rp27,942 (+14.6%).
challenges.answer: Set FY2030E and lt to the 0.835 rule and extended the explicit series to FY2031E-FY2033E so every forecast year equals 0.835 of revenue per tonne. The rule now gives Rp16.79m, not Rp16.45m, because volume is held flat at 1.56 Mt and realisation is 0.8935; the old Rp16.45m was computed on the 1.70 Mt path. Verified in the packet: unit_cost/revenue per tonne = 0.835 in all eight forecast years.

challenges.challenge: Scenario values are incoherent with tp_base. Mirrored -20%/+20% CPO shocks produce bull v0 of Rp23,076 (+5.2% against base Rp21,926) and bear Rp13,522 (-38.3%), which is not a mirrored distribution. Re-running the same volume and cost shocks on a deck scaled multiplicatively in values, lt and spot gives bull Rp34,390 and bear Rp15,254, putting the probability-weighted target at roughly Rp25,300-26,700, not Rp21,693. The cause is that _apply_overrides writes shocked values back into the deck while deck_value interpolates, so the post-FY2029 path is pinned flat and loses its 3.28% lt escalation; the bull's premium decays from 1.20x to 1.12x and its EBITDA falls every year after FY2029.
challenges.answer: The engine override defect is real and is escalated to OPS: scripts/ is outside the analyst's writable scope, so the deck-scaling fix could not be applied here. The scenario price shock is instead applied through a.realisation (x0.8 bear, x1.2 bull), which is the same revenue path as scaling the deck because revenue = volume x realisation x benchmark, and it leaves the reviewed deck on its escalating path. Rerun after the capex normalisation: bear v0 Rp14,379 (-29.6% vs base Rp20,409) and bull Rp27,605 (+35.3%), against +5%/-38% before; tp_weighted Rp22,337. Each scenario's FY2033 realised price equals the base path times its shock.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF reports factor 0.93813 with an implied FY2027 CPO of US$1,163.28 as the deck that reproduces the Rp9,500 price. A correctly scaled deck at 0.93813 yields a DCF of Rp15,529, not Rp9,500; the true factor is about 0.873 (implied FY2027 about US$1,081). The headline claim that the market applies only a 6% haircut to a fair deck is therefore false: the implied haircut is about 13%. The bisection runs on the flattened path while implied_value is computed from the original deck, so the two numbers do not describe the same scenario.
challenges.answer: The wrong factor (0.93813) and implied price (US$1,163) are removed from the Investment summary and §4; the report states the reverse-DCF direction without a point factor. The engine's reverse_dcf field still bisects on the flattened post-FY2029 path (the _apply_overrides defect, outside the analyst's writable scope and escalated to OPS), so the true factor is computed independently on the correctly escalating deck by shocking a.realisation: factor 0.905, implied FY2027E CPO US$1,122/t and long-run marker US$1,041/t against the deck's US$1,150. The extreme_call justification now carries those numbers and the engine caveat.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states the DCF terminal value is 0.6% of the total and that it uses a 0.0% nominal rupiah growth rate. fund record records tv_share 0.58855 and g 0.04, and the terminal value is 58.9% of the enterprise value. The two inputs that drive most of the primary method are described as the opposite of what the model uses, a 100x unit error on the terminal share and a 4pp error on growth.
challenges.answer: The 0.6% and 0.0% were a formatter error: pctv printed a fraction already in percent. Both placeholders now use pct, so §4 and §5 print the model's terminal share (55.1% of EV after the capex normalisation) and a 4.0% nominal rupiah growth rate, and the text states the terminal is a Gordon perpetuity at 4%.

challenges.challenge: The 0.835 cost/revenue ratio is calibrated on 9M-2026, when EBITDA margin was 16.6%, the best of the last five years; FY2022-25 EBITDA margins were 12.7%, 8.3%, 14.1% and 13.5%. Holding that peak ratio for eight years and the perpetuity is the single largest driver of the target and is presented as a mechanical fact rather than a peak-margin assumption. The cost series also escalates at 2.5% while revenue escalates at 3.28% (lt_escalation: idr), so the modelled margin rises about 0.8pp a year without limit.
challenges.answer: Every forecast year is now set to 0.835 of revenue per tonne, so cost escalates with revenue instead of 2.5% against 3.28%. The checkable cash-cost ratios are 0.827 in FY2024, 0.849 in FY2025 and 0.833 in 9M-2026, so 0.835 is mid-range, not the peak; the higher 9M-2026 EBITDA margin comes from price and lower opex, not from a peak cost ratio. FY2022 and FY2023 cannot be computed on the same basis because the data pack's D&A for those years is the direct-method figure (Rp156.6bn and Rp165.9bn), and the law forbids calibrating a cash cost off an unchecked D&A; the older LK is not in the source set.

challenges.challenge: The calibration.ebitda justification argues the cost is price-linked, but the model implements no such linkage: cost_per_bcm is a hardcoded IDR per tonne for each year. At FY2025 prices the model prints Rp2,094bn of EBITDA against Rp3,880bn actual (-46%) because the FY2026 cost is set off the FY2026 price. The gate is flagging a real mis-specification, and the justification describes a mechanism the engine does not have.
challenges.answer: The gate is flagging a real limitation: the commodity template has no price-linked cost input (unit_cost = strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm + other_cost_unit), so the FY2026 cost is set off the FY2026 price and the gate's FY2025 re-pricing lifts the cost ratio to 0.94 and overstates cost. The earlier justification's claim that FY2025 FX and opex made the gate print Rp4,258bn was wrong (the same run prints Rp451bn) and has been removed. The justification now states the limitation, shows the checkable ratios (0.833, 0.849, 0.827) and the 9M-2026 margin reproduction, and escalates a template cost-ratio input to OPS.

challenges.challenge: The ageing tree profile (average age just under 16 years) and the company's FY2026 FFB target of 3.8 Mt, below FY2025's 3.822 Mt, are described but not modelled. Volume is instead raised from 1.56 Mt to 1.70 Mt by FY2030 on 5,080 ha replanted in 2025 and 8,000 ha planned, which is 2.9% of the estate a year and cannot yield for several years. The bear case cuts volume only 5% and contains no FFB yield shock.
challenges.answer: Volume is held flat at 1.56 Mt (FY2027E 1.54 Mt on the El Nino), with no 1.70 Mt uplift: the 5,080 ha replanted in 2025 and 8,000 ha planned are 1.8% and 2.9% of the 280,325 ha estate and take years to bear, and the company's own FY2026 FFB target of 3.8 Mt is below FY2025's 3.822 Mt. The bear case now carries a deeper FFB-yield shock, volume x0.90, mirrored by x1.10 in the bull.

challenges.challenge: The November-2026 export charge cut of US$61.9/t to US$246.4/t, about -20%, is cited as a realisation tailwind but realisation is held at 0.8755 in every year and every scenario. A roughly 6% lower wedge on the reference price is a first-order uplift to the realised price and is absent from the base, the bull and the sensitivity grid.
challenges.answer: The cut is quantified and carried into the base: the combined charge falls US$61.9/t to US$246.4/t, and with 36% of volume exported the blended realised price gains 0.36 x US$61.9 = US$22.3/t, or 2.05% of the FY2027E realised price. Realisation rises to 0.8935 from FY2027E (0.8785 in FY2026E for two months of the cut), and the scenarios inherit it.

challenges.challenge: The bull narrative promises 'restoring the FY2022 margin', but the constant 0.835 cost ratio caps EBITDA margin near 16% in every year and every scenario, so the model cannot produce the bull it describes. Separately, the Rp5,792bn of cash is 32% of market cap and earns 7-8.6% inside the DCF; the report never argues that a distribution or buyback would create value.
challenges.answer: The bull narrative no longer promises a return to the FY2022 margin; it now says the constant cash-cost ratio keeps the margin honest while price and volume drive EBITDA. The Rp5,792bn of cash is carried at face in the net-debt bridge, and §4 states that no distribution is assumed because none is announced, while a buyback at today's price would be accretive and is an upside risk.

challenges.challenge: The report says the 7.07x multiple is applied to 'FY2026E earnings', but the method computes 7.0696 x FY2025A EBITDA of Rp3,879.9bn, plus cash, minorities and associates, giving Rp17,075. Applied to FY2026E EBITDA of Rp4,984.5bn the same method gives about Rp21,132, worth about +Rp1,014 on the blended v0 (+4.6%).
challenges.answer: The prose now says the peer-median EV/EBITDA multiple is applied to FY2025A EBITDA, matching the model's current 6.66x on Rp3,880bn. The commodity method card forbids capitalising a forecast cyclical peak, and FY2026E sits at the deck's high point, so the last audited year is the correct through-cycle base for a cross-check.

challenges.challenge: The P/B cross-check applies the 1.60x peer median to book while the report argues it is right because ROE is 'close to' the cost of equity. ROE FY2026E is 10.0% against COE 11.2% and g 4.0%, which justifies about 0.83x book (Rp10,500), not 1.60x (Rp20,208). The cross-check sits about 92% above its own justified multiple and adds roughly Rp1,450 to the blended target.
challenges.answer: The peer-median P/B is not a justified multiple for AALI: ROE is below COE, so the ROE/COE-implied multiple is below book while the peer median is about twice it. We cut the P/B weight from 15% to a token 5% and say so in §4, so the cross-check no longer drives the blend; the DCF and EV/EBITDA carry 95%. The blend sensitivity is shown by the scenario table and the sensitivity grid.

challenges.challenge: Capex is Rp911bn in FY2033 against D&A of Rp1,875bn, only 49%, yet FCFF grows at 4% nominal in perpetuity. The report concedes the asset base is being consumed faster than it is renewed but does not charge the replacement gap. Closing it to D&A would cut FY2033 FCFF by about 27% and, at a 58.9% terminal weight, the DCF by about 16%.
challenges.answer: The gap is real: the accounts are historical-cost (S4 note 2a), fixed-asset additions ran at Rp330.4bn against depreciation of Rp979.4bn in FY2025 and Rp411.8bn against Rp936.3bn in FY2024 (S4 note 12), and the fixed-asset block is 60% depreciated (gross Rp19.7tn, net book Rp7.78tn). The bearer-plant leg is funded (replanting cash additions close to bearer-plant amortisation), so the under-investment is in fixed assets. We keep the company's actual programme through FY2030E and ramp the fixed-asset leg from FY2031E so total capex equals D&A in FY2033E and the perpetuity is struck on a renewed base. Impact: DCF Rp25,572 to Rp22,173 (-13.3%), terminal share 59.7% to 55.1%, target Rp24,857 to Rp22,337, total return 170% to 143%. We also corrected the previous claim that the assets were revalued: the LK is historical cost.

missing_bull_case.note: The November-2026 export charge cut (US$61.9/t, about -20%) is called a realisation tailwind but realisation is held at 0.8755 in every year and every scenario, so a sourced first-order uplift never reaches the model or the bull case. The fixed ~16% margin also makes the bull narrative's 'FY2022 margin' unreachable, and the value of the Rp5,792bn cash is never argued as a return-of-capital catalyst.

missing_bear_case.note: The ageing tree profile (average age just under 16 years) and the company's own FY2026 FFB target of 3.8 Mt, below FY2025's 3.822 Mt, are described but never modelled: volume still rises from 1.56 Mt to 1.70 Mt by FY2030 on 5,080 ha replanted in 2025 and 8,000 ha planned, which is 2.9% of the estate a year with a multi-year immature period. The bear cuts volume only 5% and assumes unit cost falls 15% with price, ignoring FFB price stickiness on the downside.

assumption_realism.note: The 0.835 cash-cost/revenue ratio is calibrated on 9M-2026, the best margin of the last five years (16.6% EBITDA against 12.7%, 8.3%, 14.1% and 13.5% in FY2022-25), then held for eight forecast years and the perpetuity. The cost series itself violates the stated rule at FY2030 (Rp17.043m against Rp16.453m per tonne) and escalates at 2.5% while revenue escalates at 3.28%, so the modelled margin drifts up about 0.8pp a year forever.

evidence_and_citations.note: The realisation numerator, FY2025 CPO and derivative revenue of Rp25,522.6bn, is cited to F3, which is the production table (1,473 kt); the number exists at S4 note 29 but no fact carries it. The 9M-2026 EBITDA of Rp3,925bn and Rp1,905bn of parent profit are computed, not printed, and have no fact. By contrast the 14% related-party share is correctly sourced to S3 page 33 (3,273,957 of 23,714,321), and the export levy, domestic CPO and cash facts check out.

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF frame, net-debt/minority/associate bridge and peer set are appropriate, but three numbers are wrong. The reverse DCF factor of 0.93813 actually produces Rp15,529, not Rp9,500. The scenario deck path is flattened. The P/B cross-check applies 1.60x when ROE 10.0% against COE 11.2% and g 4.0% justifies about 0.83x. Section 4 also reports a terminal share of 0.6% (actual 58.9%) and g of 0.0% (actual 4.0%).

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is measured and credits the data-pack repair, but the 135% headline rests on the reverse DCF and the scenario weighting, both numerically broken. Section 1's '3.0x EV/EBITDA' uses FY2026E while the ev_ebitda method uses FY2025A. The bear's 25% probability is asserted, not anchored to a base rate or to the frequency of 20%-plus CPO drawdowns.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model reads d.agri.cpo in USD/t with an IDR cost base, unit_factor 0.001, zero royalty and the export-wedge realisation, matching PGUN and JARR and the deck's lt_escalation of idr. FY2026E 1,135, FY2027E 1,240, FY2028E 1,210, FY2029E 1,180 and lt 1,150 all match the reviewed agri deck. The flattening is an engine defect, not a misread of the deck.

conservatism_audit.note: Two unjustified conservatisms: realisation held flat at 0.8755 despite the sourced levy cut, and ev_ebitda applied to FY2025A EBITDA of Rp3,880bn rather than the FY2026E Rp4,984bn the text claims, worth about Rp1,014 a share on the blend. Two unjustified optimisms: P/B at 1.60x against 0.83x justified, and the peak 9M-2026 cost ratio held for eight years. The net effect of the four is not shown.

calibration.note: Both BLOCK flags are marked justified, but the calibration.ebitda justification describes a price-linked cost mechanism the model does not implement: cost_per_bcm is a hardcoded IDR per tonne each year. At FY2025 prices the model prints Rp2,094bn of EBITDA against Rp3,880bn actual (-46%) because the FY2026 cost is set off the FY2026 price, so the gate is flagging a genuine mis-specification. The extreme_call drivers are sourced, but its reverse DCF is wrong.

signoff.notes: APPROVED. The substance holds. QC round 2 recomputed FY2025A EBITDA 3,879.9, 9M-2026 EBITDA 3,925.6, net cash 5,792.2 and volume, and the four BLOCK and one WARN gates are justified the way the packet prints them.
